prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle in bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle graphene, opening the field of moire quantum matter.

statement.case_for: I keep magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene (B001) alone, with MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Bistritzer. The round-1 exchange did not change the core of my case: a quantitative continuum-model prediction (2011) fixed a magic angle where the bands flatten, and experiments in 2018 found correlated insulators and superconductivity in that regime. Since then independent groups have reproduced the phases and extended them to twisted multilayers, moire TMDs and fractional Chern insulators. As a statistical physicist I find the most persuasive point is that interaction strength became a tunable control parameter, set by geometry and gating, which gives theory a clean, falsifiable platform. The existence of the flat-band correlated phases does not depend on the pairing mechanism, so the discovery is mature after eight years. Three-name attribution holds up against the round-1 files: six members now prefer this configuration, and nobody has argued that the two-author prediction can be split. I do not treat the count as evidence; I treat the independent reproduction and the sharpness of the prediction as the evidence.
statement.case_against: The strongest remaining reservation is the experimental credit. Jarillo-Herrero is the only experimental name, while Cao (first author of the 2018 papers), Fatemi and the Dean, Efetov, Young and Yazdani groups fall outside the three-name limit, and earlier twisted-graphene band-structure theory (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto, Suarez Morell) has precedence claims the citation must be worded around. The second reservation is maturity: the pairing mechanism and several correlated states are still debated, and twist-angle disorder complicates interpretation. I take Kroll and Lindroth seriously that a citation resting on interpretation would be risky, which is why the citation names only the prediction and the observation of the phases. If the committee decided the open interpretation was disqualifying this year, B007 is the sound fallback.

responses.point: Kroll holds B007 first on cleanliness of attribution and a finished capability with stable interpretation, and asks whether my concern about B001 is topical or scientific; he also asks the B001 side to name its deciding criterion.
responses.response: The criterion that decides it for me is a tested prediction opening a new class of tunable matter, not capability versus discovery in the abstract. I agree B007 has the cleaner attribution and I rank it as my first alternative, so this is not a doubt about its science. But the discovery in B001 is the flat bands and the phases found at the predicted angle, and those are reproduced across groups, so Kroll's maturity argument against the mechanism sets a stricter bar than for an experimental discovery in general. His point that the SI redefinition remains pending is a similar open item for B007, and I would not use either as decisive. My answer to his question is that my preference is scientific, not topical, and that I would accept B007 without objection if the committee came to weight attribution cleanliness above field-opening breadth.

responses.point: Lindroth keeps the lattice clock first, argues the interpretation of the correlated states is not stable enough to base a citation on, and says the clock is distinct from the 2005 comb and the 2012 ion-control prizes.
responses.response: I accept her distinction from the comb prize: the magic-wavelength lattice is a separable idea and a real invention, so I do not count the earlier prizes against B007. On stability, I think the difference is in what we are asking the citation to say. Mine says nothing about the pairing mechanism; it states a prediction at a magic angle and the observation of correlated insulating and superconducting states, which are not contested. If the citation were written around an explanation I would share her concern. Her point about the asymmetry of attribution is fair, and the thin experimental side of B001 is my main remaining discomfort. I do not think it is large enough to make me change my first choice, but it is the reason I keep B007 as my first alternative and not lower.

responses.point: Danielsson argues that the citation must credit the prediction and the observed phases and not claim an explanation of superconductivity, and that naming one experimental leader is a defensible convention.
responses.response: I agree with the wording constraint and have kept it in my citation. On the convention, I accept that a laureate leading the discovery group is how committees have usually handled this, but I would keep the imbalance on record rather than pretend that it is resolved: three names cannot reflect Cao, Fatemi and the other groups. I am glad he is firm about not dropping Bistritzer, since the magic-angle calculation is the statement the experiments tested.

responses.point: Olsson separates the attribution risk on the theory side, where earlier twisted-graphene band-structure work exists, from the independent experiments, which she treats as evidence of maturity, and notes that a three-name B001 leaves no room for a second part.
responses.response: I think her split is right: independent experiments are evidence of robustness, while the precedence question is a theory-side one. I would answer it in the citation wording, by crediting the continuum-model prediction of flat bands at a magic angle and not twisted graphene in general, and I would acknowledge the earlier band-structure work in the committee's background documentation. I also accept her point that a three-person B001 excludes a second part; since B007 also needs two names, I do not see a two-part configuration that avoids cutting either Bistritzer or the experimental leader, and I would not make that cut.

responses.point: Eriksson reads B001 as a prediction tested in nature and asks whether the prize would rest on a single subfield, with B007 as a more mature, less contested achievement.
responses.response: I agree that the prediction-and-test structure is the strongest feature, and I accept that this is a single-subfield prize. I do not think subfield balance should drive the choice, because a statistical-physics reading of the problem finds the same logic in B001 as in the better-known cases: a simple model that identified the control parameter. He is right that B007 is more mature and less contested; that is the reason I keep it as my first alternative and not just a fallback.

uncertainties: How much weight a committee should give the unresolved pairing mechanism and the twist-angle variability when judging timing, even though the existence of the phases is robust.
Whether the single experimental name is defensible given Cao, Fatemi and other groups outside the three-name limit, and how the citation should handle earlier twisted-graphene band-structure theory.
Whether the committee will, in the end, weight attribution cleanliness and maturity (B007) above field-opening novelty (B001); I would accept B007 without objection.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my disclosure. My profile documents no personal or institutional connection to MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero or Bistritzer, nor to Katori, Ye or the B008 names. My own work (inertial particles in turbulence, stochastic dynamics, random matrices, neural networks) is outside condensed-matter physics and outside every shortlisted entry, so I judge B001 and B007 as an interested outsider. I note the disclosures of Kroll (Hall laboratory, JILA link to Jun Ye on B007), Johansson (field proximity to B058) and Olsson (B030 and a possible link to Katori). I think Kroll's is a matter for disclosure and the pair Katori and Ye is uncontested, which does not change my ranking.
